unit.title: Subjunctive: doubt & denial
unit.subtitle: When you're not sure: no creo que, dudo que, es imposible que

grammar.title: Certainty stays; doubt flips
grammar.intro: Here's the elegant rule of this unit. When you believe something is true, the verb stays in the indicative (the normal form). But the moment you doubt or deny it, the verb flips to the subjunctive. The same idea, plus or minus certainty, changes the mood entirely.

sections.heading: The key contrast: creo que vs no creo que
sections.body: This pair is the heart of the unit. Creo que (I think) states a belief → indicative. No creo que (I don't think) casts doubt → subjunctive.

ex.en: I don't think he's coming today.

sections.heading: Doubt & denial triggers
sections.body: These openers all express doubt or deny a fact, so they all take the subjunctive:

sections.heading: Maybe: quizás & tal vez
sections.body: Quizás and tal vez both mean maybe. Because they signal genuine uncertainty, they usually take the subjunctive — the more unsure you are, the more natural it sounds.

takeaways: Belief → indicative: creo que viene. Doubt → subjunctive: no creo que venga.
Doubt/denial triggers: no creo que, dudo que, es imposible que, no es verdad que, no pienso que.
Common irregulars here: venga, sea, sepa, esté, tenga.
Quizás / tal vez usually take the subjunctive: quizás llueva.

mistakes.why: No creo que expresses doubt, so the verb goes subjunctive: venga, not viene.
After 'dudo que', ser flips to the subjunctive: sea, not es.

mistakes.w: No creo que venga… creo que venga.
mistakes.why: When you DO believe it (creo que), keep the indicative: viene, not venga.
